item.title: Helping the web archive itself
item.description: Rosen shares Dave Winer's call to help the web preserve itself and links to Jay Rosen's Internet Archive as his own contribution.

item.title: Where can readers find the citizens agenda itself?
item.description: After James Brooks describes an Alaska Beacon decision guided by a citizens agenda, Rosen asks where the site presents the agenda itself rather than commentary about it.

item.title: Josh Marshall on platform audiences
item.description: Rosen shares Josh Marshall's distinction between Bluesky users' expectations and the belief among some X users that they encounter a representative population. Rosen corrects Marshall's name in a later post.

item.title: Correcting Josh Marshall's name
item.description: Quoting his earlier post about platform audiences, Rosen corrects the attribution from the misspelled name in that post to Josh Marshall.

item.title: News marketing and the promise of insider access
item.description: In the opening post of a two-part argument, Rosen questions news subscription imagery that promises readers greater access to an inner circle.

item.title: Two meanings of journalism's inner circle
item.description: Continuing his post about news subscription imagery, Rosen distinguishes reporting that makes readers feel present from a paid promise of knowledge withheld from others.

item.title: A community's bond with the Lexington Herald-Leader
item.description: Rosen recommends a city council member's speech after newsroom cuts at the Lexington Herald-Leader as evidence of a newspaper's community bond and independence.

item.title: The 60 Minutes premiere and its audience decline
item.description: Rosen shares Status's comparison of the 60 Minutes premiere audience with the previous year and points to an accompanying view of the decline.

item.title: Opinion writers, audiences, and newsroom managers
item.description: Rosen argues that opinion writers with their own brands and audiences limit managers' power. He recommends Eric Deggans's account of why Karen Attiah's victory matters.

item.title: What are your top issues in November’s elections? Inform Roanoke Times coverage
item.description: The Roanoke Times asks readers which issues matter most so those concerns can guide its fall election coverage. Jay Rosen cited the project as a current Citizens Agenda example.

item.title: Citizens Agenda '26: Help CDN pin down candidates on issues that matter to you
item.description: Jon Bauer explains how Cascadia Daily News is using the Citizens Agenda model for a fifth election season in Whatcom and Skagit counties. Readers submit and rank questions that reporters will put to candidates, shifting coverage toward voter priorities, engagement, and solutions rather than campaign horse-race narratives.

item.title: Why The Ubyssey is covering the World Cup
item.description: The Ubyssey sports editor Caleb Peterson applies Jay Rosen’s concept of “awayness” to the newspaper’s decision to cover the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Peterson argues that simply reporting events readers can already watch or find elsewhere does not solve an awayness problem; the publication instead has to add value through beat expertise, analysis and trusted voices.

item.title: Jay Rosen’s Internet Archive: an Introduction.
item.description: Jay Rosen introduces the archive of his online work and identifies Joe Amditis as its developer and curator. The Q&A explains what counts as a record, the limits of link-based preservation, and how readers might use the collection.

item.title: Subscribers buy a product. Members join the cause.
item.description: PressThink essay in which Rosen draws a distinction at the heart of journalism's funding debate: subscribers buy a product, members join the cause -- one a transaction, the other a commitment. Drawing on his 2017-2021 Membership Puzzle Project and Talking Points Memo's membership drive, he contrasts subscription models (Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, New York Times's "journalism worth paying for") with membership models such as the Salt Lake Tribune's decision to drop its paywall and treat trustworthy journalism as a right, not a luxury. He argues membership is about solidarity with a cause -- increasingly, chronicling an authoritarian crisis -- and predicts that donating one's knowledge and civic skills will become common practice in journalism.

item.title: News Consumers are Content Creators in an AI-Driven World
item.description: The lines between news consumers and content creators are fading because of artificial intelligence. This shift began with the rise of the internet, social media, and smartphones, leading to participatory journalism and citizen reporting. AI tools now amplify this trend, providing automated content generation, media editing, and personalized curation, along with potential for fact-checking. Consumers are also curators and gatekeepers, influencing the visibility of information through their interactions. This new reality brings responsibilities, including combating misinformation, understanding AI's role, and promoting media literacy. The future of news involves active consumer participation, offering opportunities for a diverse information landscape alongside challenges in maintaining accuracy.
